How many FPS are you getting? If there's no FPS cap in place or the monitor refresh rate isn't being reached (when V-Sync is enabled), then it's expected for the GPU to be fully utilized unless there's a CPU bottleneck. This can lead to high temperatures and fan noise, which is why you always want either V-Sync or a FPS cap with the **Max FPS** project setting.

Running flat-out without any cap should only be done for benchmarking purposes, it's a worse gaming experience all around ([you actually get *higher* input lag if you are GPU-limited](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=msOWcvoIC8M&pp=ygUWYmF0dGxlbm9uc2Vuc2UgZnBzIGNhcA%3D%3D)).
@Calinou If "running flat out" should be only for benchmarking, then why doesn't Godot default to V Sync + FPS cap on?

> How many FPS are you getting? If there's no FPS cap in place or the monitor refresh rate isn't being reached (when V-Sync is enabled), then it's expected for the GPU to be fully utilized unless there's a CPU bottleneck. This can lead to high temperatures and fan noise, which is why you always want either V-Sync or a FPS cap with the **Max FPS** project setting.

At most, I get 2000 FPS - why are you saying it's expected that the GPU will be fully utilized? At the very least, that shouldn't happen. If your scene isn’t changing, it only has five light sources, and you're getting over 1000 FPS, then to me that's already unhealthy behavior. That actually supports my suspicion about uneven GPU utilization.

> Running flat-out without any cap should only be done for benchmarking purposes, it's a worse gaming experience all around ([you actually get _higher_ input lag if you are GPU-limited](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=msOWcvoIC8M&pp=ygUWYmF0dGxlbm9uc2Vuc2UgZnBzIGNhcA%3D%3D)).

> [@Calinou](https://github.com/Calinou) If "running flat out" should be only for benchmarking, then why doesn't Godot default to V Sync + FPS cap on?

I also noticed that V-Sync is selected automatically in some projects. I don’t get any stuttering without V-Sync, but it’s strange that you're saying it's only for benchmarking - in other engines and the huge number of games I’ve played, I’ve never seen that to be the case. That causes dissonance for me. V-Sync wasn’t designed for regular gameplay - it was made so that I could cap the FPS to match my 70Hz monitor, nothing more. When it’s disabled, there’s simply no cap. But you're saying I should use V-Sync. I know many people who deliberately disable it because it limits the frame rate. Again, this creates a contradiction for me - as I understand from your statements, the real issue lies in uneven load distribution.

--

I tested the behavior with an FPS cap, and it helps just like V-Sync. So it really does seem like the issue is that the frames are trying to push the GPU to its limits without any kind of frame rate restriction. But again - isn’t it the engine’s job to detect that and avoid maxing out the GPU unnecessarily? That seems like a logical responsibility for any engine.

Your GPU has a heat limit of 110 so going up to 100 when running uncapped is very well within spec for that GPU and expected.

> But again - isn’t it the engine’s job to detect that and avoid maxing out the GPU unnecessarily? That seems like a logical responsibility for any engine.

No. When you turn off the limiter it is not the engines job to fix "summer" and a mediocre GPU cooling solution on hardware.

If you run anything at uncapped frame rate you run it at uncapped frame rate. If your hardware can not heat handle uncapped frame rate while not being hold back by a CPU bottlenecked that is a hardware issue, not an engine issue.

That is like removing the speed limiter from your motorbicycle and complaining that you crash because your bike or you could not handle the next turn at that speed level, trying to make that crash a responsibility of the manufacturer.

Yes, you're right that 110°C is the limit, but at that point it's already critical - in fact, it shouldn't be running above 100°C. In my case, the GPU hit 100% utilization due to a maximum load, and the problem is that so far, this is the only thing that pushed it that hard. As I said, even large AI models didn’t utilize the GPU as heavily as this tiny example.

I understand your point that you're limiting things manually via FPS caps. But I still believe the engine should be capable of handling this. This isn’t a problem with the GPU or my code - the issue is that without limits, the engine consumes all available resources. Doesn’t the engine see that it’s doing this? Isn’t Godot responsible for rendering, and isn't this its load?

So yes, you can shift the blame onto the developer, but it's obvious that this should be handled out of the box. Again, it's one thing to manually remove a speed limiter from a motorcycle - that’s a deliberate engine modification at the very least - but another thing entirely when the motorcycle comes with built-in limits and is designed to throttle your speed excesses automatically.

@miruji GPU load is not an effective measuring tool for anything. By hyper-focusing on GPU load, you are unable too understand what is good and bad for performance.

A 100% GPU load means that your GPU is working as hard as it can. In practice this means that:
1. The GPU is running at its full clock rate
2. The GPU is never stalled waiting for data from the CPU

For games, we work very hard to make sure that the game engine can fully utilize your GPU. Its a big problem for gamers if they purchase an expensive GPU and then cannot reach 60 FPS in game because the GPU is not being utilized. In other words, I would rather my GPU be at 100% and reach 60 FPS, then for my GPU to be at 50% and only manage 30 FPS. 

Vsync limits your GPU from working if it rendering faster than the refresh rate of your monitor. This is great for 2 reasons:
1. It saves energy + heat if your GPU is capable of rendering faster than the refresh rate (i.e. it decreases the GPU load below 100%)
2. It allows you to use double or triple buffering to avoid tearing. 

When you disable Vsync and leave FPS uncapped, you are explicitly telling the engine you want to render as many frames per second as possible. This will naturally either max out your CPU or your GPU and your FPS will be determined by which gets bottlenecked first. In your case here, the GPU is bottlenecked first and reaches 100% utilization before the CPU does. 

The solution to avoid 100% utilization is to add a frame cap or enable vsync. This is common practice on mobile devices like the SteamDeck where you may limit FPS to 24 or 30 in order to save battery. 

When running AI models you will almost always be limited by memory bandwidth. Its true that AI models stress the GPU, but they aren't nearly as optimized as game engines. So in practice, the GPU spends a lot of time waiting for memory transfer. Therefore, it is very uncommon for AI models to reach 100% GPU utilization. In contrast to your guess, the fact they cannot reach 100% GPU utilization is actually an indicator that they are _unoptimized_ not that they are optimized. Your GPU is capable of running the AI models much faster, but because they are bottlenecked by memory bandwidth, they run slowly. 

In summary here are your options:
1. Disable Vsync and uncap FPS -> 100% utilizations is expected
2. Enable Vsync and uncap FPS -> 100% utilization is expected if the game can't reach the monitor refresh rate otherwise Utilization will be below 100%
3. Disable Vsync and cap FPS -> 100% utilization is expected if the game can't reach the FPS cap otherwise Utilization will be below 100%

In your case, I suggest setting an FPS cap at around 500 or so. This will allow you to turn off Vsync and still have a reasonable GPU load. 

> @Calinou If "running flat out" should be only for benchmarking, then why doesn't Godot default to V Sync + FPS cap on?

@Zireael07 it does... This user disabled it because they wanted uncapped FPS.

@clayjohn 

Thank you for your response - many things are clear to me now, but I believe you may have misunderstood my main point. It's not about lacking GPU power - optimization is not the issue here. The issue is that when you have a small scene and Godot detects that, why can't it automatically limit the load?

It would be logical to have, for example, a checkbox to enable a mode where this kind of load management happens automatically - without me manually setting limits or the player having to choose them in the settings (apart from VSync). I understand the need to fully utilize the GPU when running a AAA game - that makes sense. But when I run a scene with just five light sources, it's frankly ridiculous that I still have to manage GPU usage manually and shift that responsibility onto the player.

That’s why I proposed a new and fresh approach to this issue - as I see it. There's no need to default to saying this is a non-trivial task or to dismiss it outright - that attitude leads nowhere. If we always take that route, there will be no progress, so why even write code in the first place?

I'm not sharing this opinion because I want something for myself, but because I believe this idea deserves to be developed and at least considered. I’d completely understand if you’re busy with other tasks - but why not at least push this suggestion into the planning repository?

I understand the need to fully utilize the GPU when running a AAA game - that makes sense. But when I run a scene with just five light sources, it's frankly ridiculous that I still have to manage GPU usage manually and shift that responsibility onto the player.

This is what https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/5451 (and the [PR implementing it](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/66367)) is about 🙂
